This builds background on how stories show power, fairness, and community rules.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from different times and cultures can show shared fears (being punished unfairly, being powerless) and shared values (cleverness, fairness, belonging).","futureLessons":"In Lesson 6 students read Chapter 2 (pp. 16-22) and look for what is explicit and what is hinted at in the museum scene. The paragraph structure and the Word Families in This Unit anchor started today will be used again in later explanatory writing in Investigation 1.","performanceTask":"The Shared Stories, Shared Lessons performance task asks students to compare characters across texts to explain shared ideas. Today's paragraph is a first small practice of cross-text comparison with evidence from two sources."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"transformation","definition":"a complete change in form, appearance, or condition (trans- = across, change; -tion = act or state of)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"isolation","definition":"the state of being alone or set apart from others","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"revelation","definition":"something surprising that is made known or revealed","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"immortal","definition":"living forever; not able to die (im- = not; mort- = death)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mortals","definition":"people who will eventually die; human beings, as opposed to gods","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"transition","definition":"a change from one idea, place, or condition to another; also a word or phrase that links ideas in writing","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"trickster","definition":"a character in a story who uses cleverness and tricks to outsmart stronger characters","tier":"support"},{"word":"conflict","definition":"a struggle or problem between a character and another character, group, or force","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 9-15 (Chapter 1)"},{"title":"The Hare and the Lion (selected excerpt), from Zanzibar Tales: Told by Natives of the East Coast of Africa","author":"translated by George W. Bateman","pages":"Teacher-selected short excerpt (about one page)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Activate students' own experiences of being blamed or underestimated and connect them to Percy's situation and to today's question about shared fears and values.","activities":[{"id":"launch-think-pair-share","title":"When No One Believes You","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think quietly for 30 seconds. Then share with a partner: Think of a story, movie, or real situation in which someone smaller or less powerful is blamed or not believed by someone in charge. How does that character feel? What might they do?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why do so many stories show a character who is less powerful than the people around them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Because it's something a lot of people worry about. Readers feel for the character and want to see how they get out of it, like using their brain instead of strength."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we will look at two characters in that exact spot: Percy Jackson in Chapter 1, and Soongoora the hare in a very old tale from East Africa. You will explain what they have in common in a short paragraph."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Take two or three shares, then move on. Accept examples from school, family, or media."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Build cumulative language power by teaching three recurring word roots (trans-, mort-, -tion) as a Word Families in This Unit anchor, and by practicing how to decode long mythological names and terms.","activities":[{"id":"lab-word-families","title":"Word Families in This Unit","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.6","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Today's six words come from three roots that will keep returning in Investigation 1: trans- (across, change), mort- (death), and the suffix -tion (act or state of). Start a class anchor chart titled Word Families in This Unit with three columns, one per root. Add to it in later lessons."},{"type":"directions","text":"Copy the anchor chart into your notebook. Under each root, write the unit words and circle the root in each: trans- (transformation, transition), mort- (immortal, mortals), -tion (isolation, revelation, transformation)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Words are built from parts. If I know the part, I can make a smart guess about a new word. Look at immortal: im- means not, and mort- means death. So immortal means not able to die. Now look at mortals. Same root, no im-. What might mortals be?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mortals are people who can die, so regular humans. It's the opposite of immortal, like the gods in myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Percy feels cut off from the people around him. Which word with -tion could name that feeling, and how does the suffix help you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Isolation. The base is isolate, which means to set apart, and -tion turns it into the noun for the state of being alone."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Percy's story may hold a transformation, a big change, and maybe a revelation, a surprise that gets revealed. You may use these words in your paragraph, but only if they are accurate."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Cap is six words per lesson. If time is short, teach one word per root and leave the rest on the chart. Keep the chart posted all unit."}]},{"id":"lab-decode-names","title":"Word Study 2: Decoding Long Names and Terms","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.2","L.6.6"],"routine":"Syllable Chunking","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Choose a long name or term from Chapter 1 or from the Hare excerpt. Clap and chunk it into syllables with a partner, write the chunks with slashes, and say it aloud together."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When a word looks scary, find the vowel sounds, split between them, and read the chunks slowly, then faster. Try Soongoora: Soon / goo / ra. Try immortal: im / mor / tal. The mort- chunk shows up in the middle."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What helps you check that you split the word in a way that sounds right?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Each chunk has a vowel sound, and when I put the chunks back together it sounds like a real word I've heard, or like how the teacher says it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Say any names from the excerpt aloud yourself first so students hear a model. Do not rush or mock mispronunciations; have the class repeat chunk by chunk."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students gather evidence from both texts, compare how Percy and Soongoora respond to powerful figures, and write an explanatory paragraph with a clear topic sentence, evidence, transitions, precise language, and a concluding statement.","activities":[{"id":"lia-model-explanatory","title":"Review and Model Explanatory Writing","minutes":4,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.f"],"routine":"Teacher Modeling","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"An explanatory paragraph has three jobs. First, a topic sentence that tells the reader exactly what you will explain. Second, relevant evidence: details from the text that prove your point, plus an explanation of how each one connects. Third, a concluding statement that follows from what you said and tells why it matters. Transitions such as similarly, in contrast, for example, and as a result keep it smooth."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Here is a model on a different topic. Topic sentence: Both a library and a park give people a place to belong. Evidence: In the library, people share books and quiet tables. Similarly, in the park, neighbors share benches and games. Conclusion: As a result, both places remind us that a community is built by sharing space. Notice the topic sentence names the idea, each detail proves it, and the last sentence explains why it matters."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word shows comparison, and which sentence is the concluding statement?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Similarly shows the comparison. The last sentence, the one starting with As a result, is the conclusion because it tells what the examples mean."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners recognize the parts of an explanatory paragraph and the language that signals each part.","sayAsk":"Point to each part of the model and have students echo its name. Use frames: The topic sentence tells ___. One piece of evidence is ___. The conclusion explains ___. Teach comparison signals: similarly, both, in contrast. Invite students to say the model in everyday words first, then in formal words.","watchFor":"If students can name the parts but not their jobs, then ask: What does this sentence do for the reader? If students confuse evidence with opinion, then ask: Could someone point to this in the text? Success: student labels topic sentence, evidence, and conclusion correctly and names one transition."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: telling the parts of a paragraph apart","tryThis":"Color-code the model: underline the topic sentence in one color, evidence in another, conclusion in a third. Have students match each color to its job."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite the model's conclusion so it adds a deeper idea about community rather than just repeating the topic."}]}]},{"id":"lia-gather-evidence","title":"Gather Evidence from Both Texts","minutes":9,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.b","W.6.9","RL.6.1","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 9-15"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Hare and the Lion (selected excerpt), Zanzibar Tales"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread Chapter 1, pp. 9-15. Annotate details that show how Percy is treated as trouble and how adults deny or dismiss his experience. Then read the Hare excerpt your teacher selected. Annotate Soongoora's lie about the honey, Simba's challenge, and the hare's escape plan, whichever appear in your excerpt. Record your best three details from each text in a two-column chart: Percy | Soongoora. Mark the page or line for each."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"The Outline asks the writer to select an excerpt. Choose a one-page portion of 'The Hare and the Lion' that includes the honey lie, the lion's challenge, and the hare's plan, and print it for students. Page numbers for Chapter 1 may vary by edition; confirm that pp. 9-15 hold the scenes about Percy being labeled trouble and not being believed."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details show that Percy is treated as trouble, and how do the adults react when he tells what he saw?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The adults act like Percy is a problem kid who is always in trouble. When he says what he experienced, they brush it off or tell him it didn't happen, so he feels like nobody listens to him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What conflict does Soongoora face with the more powerful animals?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Soongoora is small, and the powerful animals, like the lion, are angry at him over the honey. He lied about the honey, and now he has to find a way to escape being punished by someone much stronger."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.3"],"stem":"In the Hare excerpt, what conflict does Soongoora face?","choices":[{"text":"He must escape punishment from a much stronger animal, using his cleverness instead of strength.","correct":true,"rationale":"This names the power gap and the trickster's response, which is the core conflict of the excerpt."},{"text":"He wants to win a race against the other animals in the forest.","correct":false,"rationale":"A race is a common animal-tale idea, but it is not the conflict described in this excerpt."},{"text":"He is lost and trying to find his way home.","correct":false,"rationale":"Soongoora's problem is a threat from a powerful animal, not being lost."},{"text":"He is trying to make friends with the lion.","correct":false,"rationale":"The lion challenges him; the story is about escaping control or punishment, not friendship."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in locating and paraphrasing specific details from two texts.","sayAsk":"Pair students and have them point to a line, then say it in their own words. Provide frames: In Chapter 1, the adults treat Percy like ___. When Percy tells what happened, they ___. In the Hare tale, Soongoora is in trouble because ___. The lion is more powerful because ___. Allow students to sketch a quick picture for each detail before writing.","watchFor":"If students copy long sentences, then say: Close the book and tell me the idea in your words. If students retell without a page or line, then prompt: Where in the text do you see that? Success: student records three paraphrased details per text with a location for each."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing relevant details","tryThis":"Give a guiding question for each text: How is this character treated? What does the powerful figure want? Students only mark lines that answer it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a short direct quotation from each text and explain why the exact words matter (RL.6.4)."}]}]},{"id":"lia-compare-analysis","title":"Compare Power, Cleverness, and Community Rules","minutes":6,"standards":["RL.6.9","RL.6.2","RL.6.3","W.6.2.a"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, use your chart to add a third row labeled What it suggests. Discuss: What does each story suggest about power, cleverness, and community rules? Then decide on one similarity in how Percy and Soongoora respond when more powerful figures try to control or punish them, and one difference."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How are Percy and Soongoora alike in how they are treated, and how do their responses differ?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both are at a power disadvantage and are treated as troublemakers by people with more authority. Soongoora answers with a clever plan to get away, but Percy just feels frustrated and alone, since the adults don't listen."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What shared fear and what shared value do the two stories show?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The fear is being punished or blamed when you have no power. The value is that being smart and fair matters, and that a community should listen instead of just using rules to control people."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Listen for students who say both characters respond the same way. Percy has not yet used cleverness to escape in Chapter 1; the comparison is strongest when students notice both a similar problem and different responses so far."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners compare using language of similarity and difference and add detail with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Provide frames: Both Percy and Soongoora ___. Similarly, ___. In contrast, Percy ___ while Soongoora ___. Teach adverbials that add detail: quietly, in the forest, because of the honey, at school. Invite students to expand a simple sentence, such as Percy is alone, into Percy sits alone at school because adults do not believe him.","watchFor":"If students list differences only, then ask: What problem do both characters share? If students use only and, then prompt: Try similarly or in contrast. Success: student states one similarity and one difference using a comparison transition."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: moving from details to ideas","tryThis":"Ask: What do the adults or animals in power want? How does the character feel? Then complete: Both stories suggest that ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask how the lion's rules and the school's rules each define who counts as trouble, and whether either set of rules seems fair."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-paragraph","title":"Draft the Explanatory Paragraph","minutes":9,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.b","W.6.2.f","W.6.4","L.6.1","L.6.3"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Start with a topic sentence that names both characters and the idea you will explain. Then give evidence from Percy, a transition, evidence from Soongoora, and explain how they connect. Finish with a concluding statement that tells what the two stories show about power, cleverness, and community rules. Use precise words, such as dismissed or outwit, instead of vague words, such as bad or did."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a brief explanatory paragraph comparing how Percy and Soongoora respond when more powerful figures try to control or punish them. Include: a clear topic sentence, at least one detail from Chapter 1 and one from the Hare excerpt, a comparison transition, at least one precise word chosen on purpose, and a concluding statement. Underline your transitions."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Sample paragraph for the teacher, not to be shown first: Percy Jackson and Soongoora the hare both face powerful figures who try to control them, but they respond in different ways. In Chapter 1, adults label Percy a problem kid and dismiss what he says he experienced, so he is left in isolation. Similarly, Soongoora is in danger because the powerful lion is angry about the honey, and he is much weaker. In contrast, Soongoora answers with a clever escape plan, while Percy has not yet found a way to be heard. As a result, both stories suggest that people with little power fear being punished unfairly, and that fairness and being listened to matter in any community."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in writing a structured paragraph with transitions and added detail.","sayAsk":"Let students rehearse the topic sentence aloud with a partner before writing. Frames: Percy and Soongoora both ___ , but they respond differently. In Chapter 1, ___. Similarly, in the Hare tale, ___. In contrast, ___. As a result, both stories suggest ___. Encourage adverbials to add detail: at school, because of the lie, in the end.","watchFor":"If students write two separate summaries, then prompt: Where do you compare them? Add a transition. If the conclusion only repeats the topic, then ask: What do these stories show about power and community? Success: paragraph has a topic sentence, evidence from both texts, one comparison transition, and a concluding statement."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting the paragraph","tryThis":"Offer the starter: Percy and Soongoora both face ___ , but they respond by ___. Then have students write one sentence at a time and share it aloud first."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Challenge students to use one word from today's word families accurately (such as isolation or transformation) and to add a second similarity between the characters."}]}]},{"id":"lia-revise-checklist","title":"Check and Strengthen Your Draft","minutes":2,"standards":["W.6.5","W.6.2","L.6.2"],"routine":"Checklist","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Reread your paragraph and check each item. Fix one thing: a topic sentence that names both characters and the idea, relevant evidence from both texts, transitions that show comparison, precise words, a concluding statement that follows from your evidence, and correct capitalization and punctuation. Circle the one change you made."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect paragraphs as a quick formative check of W.6.2. Look first for evidence from both texts, then for a conclusion that goes beyond repeating the topic. Use what you find to plan Flex Day groups."}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how comparing characters across two texts reveals shared fears and values.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-turn-talk","title":"Shared Fears, Shared Values","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9","W.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to a partner and discuss: What fear and what value do Percy's story and Soongoora's story share? Which piece of evidence best proves it?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why does comparing two very different stories help you understand each one better?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When I see the same problem in both, like a weaker character facing a stronger one, it helps me notice what the stories are really about, not just the plot."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the performance task you will compare characters across texts to explain shared ideas. Today's paragraph was your first practice. Keep the Word Families in This Unit chart; we will keep adding to it."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Prepare for Lesson 6 by reading Chapter 2 closely.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch2","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 2","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 2","pages":"pp. 16-22"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read Chapter 2 and annotate details about Percy's behavior, Grover's nervousness, and what Mr. Brunner says. Mark one place where you think something is being hinted at but not stated.
